content:
India's Parliament will reconvene on Monday, November 30, for a special sitting expected to take up one of the most consequential constitutional changes in decades: a delimitation-linked bill that would expand the Lok Sabha from 543 to 850 seats and reserve about a third of them for women. The Union Cabinet is scheduled to meet on Friday, November 27, to consider the revised legislation before the session opens, according to [NDTV](https://www.ndtv.com/india-news/amid-delimitation-womens-quota-bill-buzz-centre-seeks-to-reconvene-parliament-from-november-30-12381318).

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced on Thursday that the government had asked Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla to reconvene the lower house on November 30 and Rajya Sabha Chairman C. P. Radhakrishnan to call the upper house on December 2. Both houses are expected to conclude their proceedings on December 3, subject to the business before them. There will be no Question Hour, Zero Hour or Private Members' Business during the sitting, according to bulletins issued by the two secretariats.

The sitting is technically an extension of the Monsoon Session, which was adjourned sine die on August 13 but was never formally prorogued. The gap between the last sitting and the reconvening will stretch to 108 days by November 30, beating the previous record of 87 days set in 2008. Because the session was never prorogued, it can be recalled at less than a week's notice, whereas a fresh summons after prorogation would have required two weeks.

At the centre of the sitting is the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which links the implementation of women's reservation to a fresh delimitation of parliamentary constituencies. The 2023 women's reservation law granted a 33 per cent quota for women in Parliament and state assemblies, but its implementation was tied to a delimitation exercise following the first census conducted after the law came into force. The proposed amendment seeks to speed up that process by allowing the redistribution of seats on the basis of the 2011 Census, or any other census selected by the government, instead of waiting for the completion of the 2027 Census.

Under the draft, the total number of Lok Sabha seats would rise from 543 to a maximum of 850. Around one-third of the expanded house — approximately 283 seats — would be reserved for women on a rotational basis. The government wants the quota in place before the 2029 general elections.

The bill is back because it failed the first time. When it was put to a vote in the Lok Sabha on April 17, 298 members supported it and 230 opposed it. With 528 votes cast, the government needed 352 for the two-thirds majority a constitutional amendment requires, and fell short by 54 votes. The defeat forced the government to withdraw the related Delimitation Bill, 2026, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026.

The arithmetic is what the past seven months of backroom politics have been about. The Lok Sabha currently has three vacancies, bringing its effective strength to 540. One assessment cited by The Shillong Times puts the ruling National Democratic Alliance's potential tally at 319 if it secures the backing of Trinamool Congress rebels and the lone Shiromani Akali Dal MP. The figure could rise to around 353 — just past the threshold — if the DMK with 22 seats, the Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar) with eight, and the YSR Congress with four also vote in favour.

That is why the regional parties hold the balance. The YSR Congress is likely to support the bill if it ensures regional balance, party sources told ANI. DMK chief M. K. Stalin has said that if the number of constituencies is increased, Tamil Nadu's share must not fall below its current 7.18 per cent under any circumstances.

The southern states' anxiety is the most sensitive part of the debate. Because delimitation redistributes seats according to population, states in the south that controlled population growth more successfully fear losing their relative share of representation to the more populous north. The government has verbally promised a formula that would increase the number of seats in every state by 50 per cent, preserving the current balance of proportion — but that assurance was not in the text of the bill defeated in April, and the opposition has seized on the gap. The government is understood to be considering writing the formula into the revised version.

The opposition, led by the Congress, argues that the women's quota is already law since 2023 and only needs to be delinked from delimitation and granted within the current setup. Aam Aadmi Party MP Sanjay Singh attacked the bill on Friday, calling it a "BJP Jitao bill" rather than a delimitation bill and warning opposition parties against supporting it. The Congress has alleged that the special sitting is aimed at manipulating constituencies to benefit the ruling BJP.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah have framed the issue as a question of justice for women. "I want to tell Rahul Gandhi: it is the resolve of the Bharatiya Janata Party and our leader Narendra Modi that the women of this country will definitely get 33 per cent reservation; you cannot stop us," Shah said on Thursday, according to ANI. Modi said on Thursday that no force could stop the delivery of justice to women, blaming "one opposition party" for the bill's defeat in April.

The stakes extend beyond the women's quota. A successful delimitation would redraw the map of Indian politics for the first time since 1976, when constituency boundaries were frozen to reward states that controlled population growth. The freeze was meant to last 25 years; it has now lasted half a century. Whatever Parliament decides between November 30 and December 3 will shape the balance of power between India's states, and between men and women in its legislature, for a generation.

The session comes at a busy moment for Indian diplomacy and domestic politics, with New Delhi also navigating a delayed trade deal with Washington, as [Global Wire reported earlier this month](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-us-trade-deal-signing-delayed-november-2026), and continued tensions with Pakistan following the Pahalgam attack, covered in [Global Wire's earlier reporting](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-pakistan-escalation-pahalgam-attack-november-2026). But the delimitation bill is the test the government has chosen for this session — and the numbers, not the rhetoric, will decide whether it passes this time.
summary: India's government has reconvened Parliament for a special sitting from November 30 to December 3, with the Union Cabinet meeting on Friday to clear a revised delimitation bill that would expand the Lok Sabha from 543 to 850 seats and reserve a third of them for women. The constitutional amendment was defeated in April for want of a two-thirds majority, and the government has spent seven months assembling the numbers to try again.
title: India calls special Parliament session from November 30 to revive delimitation-linked women's quota bill
